criterion_notes.c1: Examines household domestic water supply access across primary, tertiary, and ungazetted settlements in Ngamiland District, Botswana, including private indoor/yard connections, communal standpipes, neighbor taps, and unprotected river/stream sources.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study analyses water governance, legislative frameworks, tariff structures, and multi-agency institutional arrangements (DWA, NWDC, WUC). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, it directly examines legal/administrative eligibility and settlement recognition rules (gazetted vs. ungazetted settlement status based on the 250-person population threshold governing entitlement to public water supply), local administrative/political discretion and accommodation (connecting 30 ungazetted settlements along transmission lines in the 1990s while denying connection to Gucha to deter informal settlement growth), utility cessation of communal tap repairs to push private connections, tariff/cost-recovery rules and flat-rate unmetered billing, enforcement/disconnection practices for bill arrears, and fragmented institutional utility mandates preventing Matlapana from accessing a DWA transmission line passing through the village.
criterion_notes.c3: Mixed-methods empirical primary study conducted between February 2012 and January 2013 using a structured household questionnaire (n = 554 randomly sampled households across 8 settlements), key informant interviews, 8 focus group discussions (at least 16 participants per settlement), informal interviews, and participant observation, analyzed with SPSS cross-tabulations and thematic analysis.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household-level outcomes on water source access (piped indoor tap, yard tap, communal standpipe, neighbor tap, or unprotected surface water) across settlement categories, exclusion of ungazetted settlements from public water services, service availability and continuity over the preceding 12 months and 24 hours, outage duration, and private connection uptake.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (554 sampled households out of 1,571 listed households across 8 settlements in Ngamiland District, Botswana; household unit of analysis), rule-type exposures (settlement gazettement/recognition status, discretionary connection/refusal policies, utility jurisdiction, tariff/billing and disconnection practices), access/reliability outcomes, and cross-sectional mixed-methods study design are all clearly identified.

evidence_quotes.quote: The government has tried to ensure equitable access to water to all households in gazetted settlements. Water is accessed from communal water points (23.1%), taps on yard (46.8%), taps inside the house (10.8%) and neighbor’s taps (7.2%).
There is generally lack of equity to water supply between gazetted and ungazetted villages in the country. A gazetted settlement is entitled to services such as water, health, education and police.
As of August 2012, the Okavango Administration Authority was supplying 30 ungazetted settlements with water, including Ukusi.
In order to encourage residents to have their own private water connections, the DWA stopped repairing the communal water points.

The study uses the household as the unit of analysis. A total of 554 questionnaires were administered in 8 settlements. Household members involved in fetching of water who are between 15 and 60 years and above were interviewed.
Thirty-one percent (31%) of households did not have water from their main sources during the time of the survey.

raw_response.exposure: Legal/administrative settlement recognition status (gazetted primary and tertiary settlements entitled to public water supply vs. ungazetted settlements under 250 residents formally excluded from service entitlement), administrative/political discretion in connecting or refusing ungazetted villages along transmission lines, utility cessation of communal standpipe repairs, tariff/billing rules, disconnection enforcement, and fragmented multi-utility institutional jurisdiction (DWA, NWDC, WUC), alongside climatic/hydrological and infrastructural factors.
raw_response.outcome: Household domestic water source access (private indoor tap, yard tap, communal tap, neighbor tap, or unprotected river/stream/well water), service exclusion in ungazetted settlements, water availability/continuity from main source in the past 12 months and past 24 hours, supply interruptions, and private connection uptake.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Households in Ngamiland District, north-west Botswana (unit of analysis: household; n = 554 randomly sampled households from 1,571 listed households across 8 settlements: Maun [primary centre], Matlapana, Somelo, and Ikoga [tertiary centres], and Xobe, Samedupi, Gucha, and Ukusi [ungazetted settlements]), supplemented by key informant interviews and 8 focus group discussions (at least 16 participants per settlement).
raw_response.rationale: This empirical mixed-methods study (n = 554 household surveys, key informant interviews, focus groups, and participant observation across 8 settlements in Ngamiland, Botswana) satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain reading and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Alongside hydrological and technical factors, it directly investigates how formal legal/administrative settlement classification rules (gazetted vs. ungazetted status based on population thresholds), local political/administrative discretion in granting or refusing pipeline connections to ungazetted villages, cessation of communal tap repairs to push private connections, tariff/billing structures, disconnection enforcement, and fragmented institutional mandates (DWA, NWDC, WUC) shape household water access, exclusion, and supply continuity.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods study (structured household survey using simple random sampling within purposively and conveniently selected settlements, combined with key informant interviews, focus group discussions, informal interviews, and participant observation)
